**I. That's Me**

Listen up! Pay attention to what I'm saying, because I'm about to be inspired like Chaucer once was, and I'll unwind, in mournful rhythm, the story of Johnny Raw, my friend. This fellow, determined to carry out a reckless scheme designed to astonish everyone, dashed away toward India, riding on Old Poulter's mare.

Stomp, stomp—he traveled over the countryside! Splash, splash—he crossed the ocean! And then he began to boast loudly: "Tell me, is there anyone who rides as skillfully as I do?

"After all, I'm the fellow who charged out to defeat the armies of classical literature, and I declared that this mare was worth far more than the two horses belonging to mighty Hector.

"I knocked old Homer right off his seat of honor, landed a blow on Virgil, and set up bold Mother Bunch to replace them both.

"I rode my reddish-brown horse into France, its spirit impossible to break; there I perched upon Joan of Arc's grave and sang a gloomy song.

"I performed a strange and marvelous verse meant to bring tears to my listeners' eyes—but when I glanced over and stopped singing, I discovered they had all drifted off to sleep!

"Well, then I swore a raging oath, vowing to find some terrible payback; and to get a reaction from them, I summoned up sturdy Taffy along with his leek.

"I rode off to both Heaven and Hell, braving every kind of storm; I invented a devilish tune and heaped curses on the whole lot of them.

"Now, Proteus, you ever-shifting prophet, arise and energize my mare! Take on any form at all—except those forms that Good Taste and Nature possess."

# The Tale of Johnny Raw

Let me set out to tell the curious tale of Johnny Raw, a fellow who once conceived of the most desperate and outlandish plan: to ride all the way to Hindoostan upon the back of Old Poulter's mare. It was a scheme born of equal parts madness and ambition, and one that would carry him through misadventures both comical and strange.

From the very beginning, Johnny was not one for modesty. He boasted loudly of his superior skill in the saddle, declaring to all who would listen that no horseman alive could match him. His mare, he swore, was worth more than all the fabled horses of Hector combined—a claim so bold that it invited both laughter and disbelief from those around him.

Yet his arrogance did not stop at matters of horsemanship. With reckless confidence, Johnny turned his contempt upon the great masters of classical literature themselves. He struck down mighty Homer, delivered a blow to noble Virgil, and—in an act of supreme absurdity—cast them both aside to make room for the lowly figure of Mother Bunch. In his estimation, the humble tales of common folklore were worth more than the epics that had endured for centuries.

Undaunted, Johnny galloped onward to France, where he arrived at the tomb of Joan of Arc. There he lifted his voice and sang a mournful tale of woe and lamentation, pouring his heart into every sorrowful note. But when at last he looked up to gauge the effect of his performance, he found to his dismay that his entire audience had fallen fast asleep, utterly unmoved by his melancholy song.

Enraged by such indifference, Johnny flew into a fury and swore bitter revenge upon them all. In his wrath, he called forth dark and unnatural spirits, summoning Proteus himself from the depths. He commanded the shape-shifting god to appear before him in any form he pleased—save only the two shapes that Johnny could never abide: those of Taste and Nature.

# On a Pretentious Poet: An Analysis

This satirical poem stands as a spirited example of eighteenth-century literary mockery, deploying the venerable tradition of mock-heroic verse to deflate the inflated ambitions of its target. Rather than confronting the pretentious writer directly, the poet cloaks his ridicule in comic characterization, presenting the figure of "Johnny Raw"—a name that itself suggests inexperience and rustic naivety—mounted upon the humble beast known as "Old Poulter's mare." This pairing of a would-be literary champion with such an unremarkable and unheroic steed immediately establishes the poem's deflationary purpose. The grandeur of epic journeys, the noble mounts of classical heroes, are here reduced to a bumbling rider on a broken-down horse, and through this image the poet signals that everything to follow will be measured against the yardstick of genuine greatness and found wanting.

The chief object of the satire is a writer who presumes to attack the towering figures of the classical canon. In his arrogance, this pretender turns his pen against Homer and Virgil, the very foundations of the Western literary tradition, as though his own meager talents entitled him to sit in judgment over the masters. There is a particular absurdity in this presumption, for the poem makes clear that a writer so lacking in ability has no business criticizing those whose works have endured for millennia. The satirist exploits this incongruity mercilessly: the greater the target's contempt for the ancients, the more ridiculous he appears, since his own productions cannot bear even the faintest comparison to theirs. His "absurd literary journeys"—the grandiose poetic undertakings he embarks upon—become occasions not for admiration but for laughter, as Johnny Raw stumbles forward on his sorry mare toward destinations no reader wishes to reach.

Central to the poem's critique is the accusation that the target's poetry is not merely bad but soporific. His verses, far from stirring the passions or elevating the mind as true poetry ought, instead induce drowsiness and boredom in all who encounter them. The image of an audience lulled to sleep serves as a devastating verdict, for it suggests that the writer has failed at the most fundamental task of the poet: to engage and move his readers. What he offers as inspired composition is revealed to be tedious labor, dull and lifeless, a failure dressed in the borrowed robes of ambition. The ridicule here operates by contrast, holding up the writer's swollen self-regard against the flat reality of his achievements, and inviting the reader to share in the joke at his expense.

Beneath the comic surface, however, the poem advances a serious argument about the principles of good writing. Its deepest charge against the pretentious poet is that he has abandoned "Taste and Nature"—the twin standards by which neoclassical criticism judged all art. In place of the balance, propriety, and truthfulness that these principles demand, the target has embraced grotesque and unnatural excess, straining after effects that violate reason and good sense. His work becomes a monument to everything that disciplined art should avoid: distortion where there should be harmony, extravagance where there should be restraint, and artifice where there should be fidelity to life. By ridiculing these failings, the poet does more than mock a single rival; he affirms a whole vision of what literature ought to be, using the weapon of satire to defend the enduring values of taste against those who would corrupt them.

In sum, the poem achieves its purpose through the marriage of comic invention and critical seriousness. The figure of Johnny Raw on Old Poulter's mare provides the enduring image around which the mockery is organized, while the specific charges—the presumptuous attacks on Homer and Virgil, the sleep-inducing tedium of the verse, the abandonment of taste and nature—supply the substance of the critique. Through laughter, the satirist accomplishes what earnest argument might not: he exposes pretension for what it is and reminds his readers that true poetic greatness cannot be counterfeited by ambition alone.

# Ille, Ego, and Chaucer: Poetic Self-Fashioning Across the Ages

## The Latin Formula

The phrase *"Ille ego"* — literally "I am that one" or "That man am I" — carries a long and resonant history in Western literature. Its most famous appearance is in the disputed opening lines traditionally attached to Virgil's *Aeneid*:

> *Ille ego, qui quondam gracili modulatus avena...*
> ("I am he who once composed my song on a slender reed...")

Though many scholars doubt these lines were written by Virgil himself, they capture a powerful poetic gesture: the author steps forward to name himself, tracing his artistic evolution from humble pastoral verse to lofty epic. The formula became a template for poetic self-presentation throughout the medieval and Renaissance periods.

## Chaucer and the Classical Inheritance

Geoffrey Chaucer (c. 1343–1400), often called the "Father of English poetry," inherited and transformed this classical tradition of authorial self-consciousness. Deeply read in Latin literature — Virgil, Ovid, Statius, and Boethius — Chaucer absorbed the models by which a poet might frame his own voice and place himself within a lineage of great authors.

In works such as *The House of Fame* and *Troilus and Criseyde*, Chaucer explicitly positions himself in relation to the classical masters. At the close of *Troilus*, he sends his "litel bok" into the world with a striking act of humility:

> *"But litel book, no makyng thou n'envie,
> But subgit be to alle poesye;
> And kis the steppes, where as thow seest pace
> Virgile, Ovide, Omer, Lucan, and Stace."*

Here Chaucer performs the reverse of the confident *"Ille ego"* — rather than proclaiming "I am he," he asks his book to kiss the footsteps of the ancients. Yet the underlying impulse is the same: an acute awareness of the poet's identity and standing within a tradition.

## The Divided Self of the Poet

The tension between *ille* (that one, the third person) and *ego* (I, the first person) mirrors a central feature of Chaucer's art: his habit of splitting himself into narrator and author. In *The Canterbury Tales*, the pilgrim "Chaucer" is presented as a somewhat bumbling figure whose own tale of Sir Thopas is interrupted for being tedious — a witty distance between the writing *ego* and the represented *ille*.

This playful self-division anticipates the modern understanding of narrative persona. Chaucer, like the classical poets before him, understood that the "I" of a poem is always partly a constructed character — a figure to be observed as much as a voice to be trusted.

## Conclusion

Bringing together *ille*, *ego*, and Chaucer reveals a continuous thread in literary history: the poet's negotiation between self-assertion and humility, between the confident naming of oneself and the reverent gesture toward tradition. Chaucer stands as a pivotal figure who received the Latin inheritance of poetic self-fashioning and reshaped it in English, laying the foundation for centuries of authors who would continue to ask, in their own ways, *"Who am I, that I should write?"*

counterfactuals.output:
# The Ballad of Johnny Raw

*A Satirical Ballad, in the Antique Manner*

---

**I.**
Come listen, all ye scribbling folk,
   And lend an idle ear,
For here's the tale of Johnny Raw,
   A poet without peer.

**II.**
He never read a page of Greek,
   Nor construed Latin line,
Yet fancied he could teach the dead
   To scan a verse divine.

**III.**
He saddled up Old Poulter's mare,
   That broken-winded jade,
And swore he'd ride the wide world round
   To ply his critic-trade.

**IV.**
"I'll cross," quoth he, "the sounding sea,
   And every clime I'll roam,
To thrash the ancient bards to bits—
   And first I'll thrash old Homer!"

**V.**
So off he trots to Ilion's plain
   Upon his sorry steed,
And finds the blind old Grecian there
   A-piping some sweet reed.

**VI.**
"Ho, Homer!" cries our valiant fool,
   "Your gods are but a fudge,
Your heroes brawl like drunken grooms—
   And this," says he, "I judge!"

**VII.**
The mare, she stumbled at a stone,
   And pitched him in the ditch;
He rose all plastered o'er with mud,
   And scratched a nettled itch.

**VIII.**
Yet nothing daunted, on he spurs
   To where the Mantuan sings,
And bawls at gentle Virgil's shade
   Of shepherds, bees, and things.

**IX.**
"Your Georgics are a farmer's book!
   Your Dido weeps too long!
I'll write a truer pastoral—"
   And here he mangled song.

**X.**
The mare fell lame, the sky grew dark,
   The rain came pelting down;
And Johnny wrote three thousand lines
   To prove that Rome was brown.

**XI.**
He challenged Dante in his hell,
   And Milton in his light,
And told great Shakespeare to his face
   He couldn't spell aright.

**XII.**
But every bard he strove to sink
   Rose brighter for the blow,
While Johnny sank in his own ink,
   As all such asses do.

**XIII.**
At length the mare lay down and died
   Beneath a foreign tree,
And Johnny, weeping, ate his book—
   'Twas all his library.

**XIV.**
So here's the moral, plain and true,
   For every upstart chaw:
The classics stand a thousand years—
   But who reads Johnny Raw?

---

*Finis.*

counterfactuals.output:
# Ille Ego; or, The Bard Who Would Out-Homer Homer

*Ille Ego*—that is, in vulgar tongue,
"'Tis I, the very man!"—so Virgil sung;
And so sing I, though somewhat out of breath,
Who rode (I'll swear to it) through Heaven and Death,
And came back cheerful, with my collar clean,
To tell the parish what these parts have seen.

My name is Tomkins. Blush not, gentle Muse,
That such a name should mount the tragic shoes;
For Tomkins I was christened, Tomkins die,
Yet Tomkins holds a thunder in his eye.
I keep a shop. I deal in tape and thread.
But O, what epics riot in my head!

One evening, having supped on toasted cheese
(That treacherous meat that fathers reveries),
I flung my ledger down, I spurned my till,
And cried, "The world shall know my sovereign quill!
Let Homer bristle in his blind repose—
I'll pluck the laurel snoring from his brows!

"What did he sing? A quarrel and a wall,
Ten years of tents, one horse, and Troy's long fall.
Pooh! I have quarrelled with my wife since May,
And that's a siege would fill a longer lay.
And Virgil—prim Aeneas, pious bore,
Who wept at Dido and then loved her more—
I'll show the ancients, dead this age of ages,
How Tomkins thunders down immortal pages!"

Now, whether cheese, or whether Fate's decree,
There came a Horse where never Horse should be:
He filled the shop, he cropped a bolt of lace,
And fixed on me a philosophic face.
Pegasus, sirs!—though shabbier than the myth,
Bald in one wing and somewhat short of pith,
He knelt (a knee like some old sofa's spring)
And bade me mount and see about this thing.

I mounted. Up we went through chimney-smoke,
Past weathercocks that crowed to see the joke,
Past steeples, stars, and one surprised balloon
Whose owner cursed us roundly at the Moon.
"To Heaven!" I cried. "I'll read them there my ode,
And Milton's self shall meekly quit the road!"

We reached the gate. Saint Peter, keys in hand,
Peered through the bars and would not understand.
"A poet? Ay, we've thousands. Mind the floor;
They're stacked like herrings just behind the door.
What have you writ?" I drew my roll of rhyme.
He read one page—and yawned the space of time.

"My friend," quoth he, and gently shut the wicket,
"We ask for genius here; you've brought a ticket.
Go down a stage. The gentleman below
Collects such works. He has a use, you know."
And so, dismissed, with dignity in tatters,
I steered my nag toward the nether matters.

Down, down we spiralled, till the air grew warm,
And Pegasus began to sweat and swarm.
Hell's porter, Cerberus (three heads, one cold),
Sniffed at my manuscript and, I am told,
Sneezed all three noses in a single blast,
Then let me by, as one whom hope had passed.

There sat old Pluto, gouty on his throne,
With Homer, Virgil—all the mighty gone!
They played at whist. They did not deign to rise.
"Another Tomkins," Homer said, and sighed.
"Read us your worst," growled Pluto, "if you dare;
We punish scansion here, and split the hair."

I read. I trembled. Reader, mark the rest:
The damned looked up—then laughed—then were not blest,
But something worse: they laughed until they cried,
And laughing so, forgot they'd ever died;
Their torments ceased; the fires forgot to burn;
The wheel of Ixion declined to turn;
And Sisyphus sat down upon his stone
And roared, and let the boulder roll alone.

Then Pluto rose. "Sir, you have broke my Hell.
No screw can pinch where such a poet fell.
You've made damnation dull, despair a jest—
Off! to the upper world, and do your worst!
Go plague the living; leave the dead in peace;
Here even Virgil's sneers begin to cease."

So back I flew. The shabby Pegasus
Set me down snoring, and departed thus,
Leaving one feather in the toasted cheese
And half a hoofprint on the ledger's leaves.
I woke. My wife stood over me with light:
"You've slept, you sot, and burnt the shop's whole night."

Yet I have seen what mortal seldom sees,
And put both Heaven and Hell to their disease;
Rejected there, unbearable below—
There is no fitter fame for verse, I trow.
So *Ille Ego*—that's the man, 'tis I,
Who bored the seraphs and out-plagued the sky;
Read on, ye ancients, tremble in your urns:
Where Tomkins rhymes, the very brimstone burns.

**The Boast of the Conquering Pen**

I rode against the classic forces,
My inkhorn brandished like a lance;
I whipped a dozen wooden horses
And swore I'd drink the wine of France.

The scholars trembled at my coming,
Their dusty tomes I split in two;
I set the sacred laurels drumming
And kicked Parnassus black and blue.

Old Homer sat upon his throne,
Blind and serene above the years—
I struck him down with quill alone
And left him weeping Grecian tears!

"Away," I cried, "your dactyls totter!
Your muse has bunions on her feet!"
I flung his epics in the water
And danced a hornpipe up the street.

Then swifter than a startled rabbit
I galloped headlong into France,
For conquest is a pleasant habit
And glory loves a gilded prance.

I found the tomb of gallant Joan,
That maid who put the crown to shame;
I clambered up and made my throne
Upon her cold and holy name.

I sat me down with lordly leisure,
I lit my pipe and crowed aloud:
"Behold the man of boundless measure,
The terror of the tuneful crowd!"

The marble did not seem to mind me,
The saints looked on without a frown—
And there, if you should care to find me,
I'm sitting still, in dead renown.

For I have routed all the ages,
Struck Homer dumb and Virgil pale,
And blotted out ten thousand pages—
Now who will stand me one more ale?

**A Tale of Sundry Bad Bookes, in the Chaucerian Manner**

Whan that Aprille with his sugred inke
Doth make the pennes of foolish poets stinke,
And every scrivener, be he ne'er so dull,
Doth thinke his brain-pan crammed and passing full—
Then longen folk to write of high romances,
And prinstout tomes wherein no Reason dances.

Ther was a Poet, wonder wroth and wide,
Who rode wel forth with Vanity for guyde;
He swore his verse dide gallop, prance, and course
As swift as ever Hector spurred his horse—
Yet all his coursers, sooth, were sadly lame,
And limped through his lines withouten shame.
"My meter thunders!" quod this doltish wight,
Whan every foot fell flatter than a mite.

He sayde his Muse was olde and passing wise,
Yclept dame Mother Bunch, of homely guyse,
Who tolde him tales beside the ale-house fire—
Of fartes and pisse and every base desire.
"Lo, heer is Arte!" he cryde with visage red,
And spued his balladës uncomely-bred.

His verses, marry, changëd every houre,
Now sweet as sugar, now as vinegar sour;
Lyk Proteus that slippeth from thy grip,
His sense wolde melte and through thy fingers slip:
One line a lion, next a bleating goot,
The thirde a fissh that swam withouten throot.
"I am so various!" boasted he ful lowde—
Nay, sir, thou'rt merely muddled, dense as clowde.

And ther cam Taffy, Welshman of the vale,
With leek upon his bonet, stoute and stale;
He rymed of "week" and "leek" and "meek" and "cheek,"
And thoughte such chyming made his fortune eke.
He stole a sonnet, as he stole (they seye)
A syde of beef upon a market-daye—
For borrowed wit doth make a thevish rime,
And plagiary is the poet's crime.

Thus alle these makers, puffed with prowde conceite,
Do fill our shelves with rubbish, rank and greet;
They praise ech other in a foolish ring,
And call it Genius when they cannot sing.
God shielde us from swich verse and swich a route—
Now Chaucer's ghost doth laugh, and putteth them oute!

*Explicit* — heer endeth this my mery jape:
Read gode bookes, or the Devil hath thy shape.
